hook: If someone close to you has been upset for weeks and you had no idea — this explains it
topic: Why familiarity creates blind spots — proximity blocks accurate perception
body:
**If someone close to you has been carrying something difficult for weeks and you had no idea — that's not a failure of caring. It's a failure of observation. And familiarity is almost always the reason.**

When we know someone well, we stop actively watching them. We think we already know what their face means. We hear "I'm fine" and we believe it — not because we're naive, but because we've built a model of that person and we're running on the model instead of the actual person in front of us.

This is one of the most painful paradoxes in long-term relationships: the closer you get to someone, the more you can start to see your assumptions about them instead of them.

Reading someone you love well requires deliberately stepping outside the story you've built about who they are. It means noticing small deviations from their normal — not from your idea of normal, from *their* normal. The way they're quieter than usual. The timing of when they laugh. Whether they're making eye contact the way they normally do.

The people closest to us are not the easiest to read. They're often the hardest — because familiarity feels like understanding, and sometimes it's the opposite.

This week: pick one person you love and watch them like you're meeting them for the first time. See what you've stopped noticing.
